## Goal

By the end, you should be able to calculate retention factors and resolution,
explain the separate roles of spacing and band width, and distinguish a
calibratable analyte area from a combined response. Work by hand first, explore
the model, then reproduce the reasoning in R.

## Background

Chromatography delays solutes through interaction with a stationary phase while
a mobile phase carries them along. A chromatogram records detector response
over time at the outlet, not position inside the column.

| Quantity | Definition in this exercise |
| --- | --- |
| Unretained transit time | $t_0$ |
| Retention factor | $k=(t_R-t_0)/t_0$ |
| Relative selectivity, B later than A | $\alpha=k_B/k_A$ |
| Resolution using **baseline** widths | $R_s=2(t_{RB}-t_{RA})/(w_A+w_B)$ |
| Gaussian width in the demo | $w_b=4\sigma$ |
| Area | Integrated response above the stated baseline; requires calibration for amount |

[IUPAC retention factor](https://doi.org/10.1351/goldbook.R05359) and
[peak resolution](https://doi.org/10.1351/goldbook.P04465) define the terminology.
A numerical resolution is not proof of purity. Peak shape, relative amount,
detector selectivity and the required accuracy also matter.

## By hand

**B1.** A has $t_R=3.00$ min and baseline width 0.40 min. B has $t_R=4.00$ min
and width 0.50 min. The unretained marker is at 1.00 min. Calculate both retention
factors, selectivity and resolution. [Hint](#hint-b1)

**B2.** Keep retention times and full areas fixed, but double both widths.
Calculate the new resolution. For ideal Gaussian peaks, what happens to height
and full integrated area? [Hint](#hint-b2)

**B3.** An integration window captures 95.45 response·min from A and 20.00 from B.
A's full area is 100.00. Calculate the combined window area and B's fraction of
it. Why is assigning the combined area to A unjustified? [Hint](#hint-b3)

**B4.** For a new pair, $t_0=0.80$ min, retention times are 2.40 and 3.20 min,
and baseline widths are 0.40 and 0.60 min. Calculate $k_A,k_B,\alpha,R_s$.
Would the same formula accept half-height widths? [Hint](#hint-b1)

## Explore {#explore}

Predict each change before touching the controls. Curves are ideal Gaussian
components with known simulation areas; the combined response is what a
nonselective detector would see. The finite window around A spans ±2σ, so it
captures about 95.45% of isolated A plus any B inside it.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="separations"></div>
<script src="../demos/dist/separations.js"></script>
```

**E1.** Check B1 at the defaults. Set the width multiplier to 2 without changing
spacing or B area. Which numbers change, and which remain fixed?

**E2.** Reset, set the spacing to 0.25 min and compare B areas 150 and 500.
Does resolution change? Does B's fraction of A's window change? Explain why a
single resolution threshold cannot establish an acceptable quantitative result.

**E3.** Hide the individual components. Could the combined curve alone tell you
the true separate areas without a justified model or additional evidence?
Export the CSV for R3, then explain what its component columns represent.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions — E1–E3"}
**E1.** Default $k_A=2$, $k_B=3$, $\alpha=1.5$ and $R_s=2.222$. Doubling widths
halves resolution to 1.111. The full areas remain 100 and 150; each Gaussian
height halves. A's ±2σ window broadens, so a neighbour can contribute more to it.

**E2.** At spacing 0.25 min the resolution is $2(0.25)/0.90=0.5556$ for both
amounts. Increasing B's area increases its contamination of the A window without
changing the retention times or widths. Therefore equal resolution can accompany
different quantitative errors. A value alone is not a purity or acceptance test.

**E3.** No. A combined response can be consistent with more than one allocation
of component areas. The exported `component_a` and `component_b` columns reveal
the simulation's construction; real data do not automatically supply them.
A model-based deconvolution would need its own assumptions and validation.
:::

## In R

Open the supplied R project and run from the project root. All inputs are
simulated. Use the existing `readr`, `dplyr` and `ggplot2` vocabulary. The raw
trace has baseline 5 response units; the demo export is already baseline-subtracted.

```r
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
peaks <- read_csv("data/course/peak-summary.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
chrom <- read_csv("data/course/chromatograms.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

**R1.** Calculate retention factors and group-wise resolution for the three
runs. Use the compound label to identify A and B, rather than row order. Save a
table with run ID, $k_A,k_B,\alpha,R_s$. [Hint](#hint-r1)

**R2.** Plot the resolved, overlap and broad traces. Explain which change causes
lost separation in each comparison. Why are the hundreds of trace rows not
hundreds of independently collected samples? [Hint](#hint-r2)

**R3.** Integrate each supplied raw trace above baseline using the trapezoidal
rule. Does total area stay constant? Optionally import the exported demo CSV
and integrate `component_a` and `component_b` separately. Explain why being able
to do this in a simulated export does not validate a real coeluting peak.
[Hint](#hint-r3)

## Hints

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint — B1 and B4" #hint-b1}
Subtract $t_0$ before dividing by it. Resolution uses the difference in retention
times and the **sum of the stated baseline widths**. All time units cancel.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint — B2" #hint-b2}
The numerator of resolution stays fixed while its denominator doubles. A
Gaussian has area proportional to height times width.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint — B3" #hint-b3}
The detector records both contributions. Divide B's contribution by the combined
window area, not by A's full area, for the requested fraction.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint — R1" #hint-r1}
Use [`mutate()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/mutate.html), then
`group_by(run)` and `summarise()`. Expressions such as `k[compound == "A"]`
identify a component within each supplied two-component run.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint — R2" #hint-r2}
Plot `response` against `time_min`, mapping `colour = run`. A time position is
part of a dependent within-run series, not another collected sample.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint — R3" #hint-r3}
For ordered times, sum $\Delta t_i(y_i+y_{i+1})/2$ after subtracting the baseline.
[`diff()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/diff.html)
returns successive differences; `head(x,-1)` and `tail(x,-1)` pair neighbours.
:::

## Solutions

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions — B1–B4"}
**B1.** $k_A=(3-1)/1=2$, $k_B=(4-1)/1=3$, $\alpha=3/2=1.5$,
$R_s=2(4-3)/(0.40+0.50)=2.222$. Using $t_R/t_0$ alone would incorrectly include
the unretained transit contribution in the retention factor.

**B2.** $R_s=2/1.80=1.111$. At fixed Gaussian area, doubling width halves height.
The full area is unchanged. A finite integration window is a different quantity:
it can exclude some A and include some B.

**B3.** Combined window area is 115.45 response·min. B contributes
$20/115.45\times 100=17.32\%$. Assigning all 115.45 to A both includes B and misses
part of A outside the window; it is not a selective measurement of A's amount.

**B4.** $k_A=2$, $k_B=3$, $\alpha=1.5$, $R_s=2(0.80)/(0.40+0.60)=1.60$.
Half-height widths require their corresponding formula/coefficient; they cannot
be substituted into this baseline-width formula unchanged.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Full worked R solutions — R1–R3"}
**R1.** Preserve component and run identities:

```r
peaks <- peaks |> mutate(k = (t_r_min - t0_min) / t0_min)
resolution <- peaks |>
  group_by(run) |>
  summarise(k_A = k[compound == "A"], k_B = k[compound == "B"],
            alpha = k_B / k_A,
            resolution = 2 * (t_r_min[compound == "B"] -
                              t_r_min[compound == "A"]) /
                          sum(baseline_width_min), .groups = "drop")
resolution
write_csv(resolution, "output/separation-resolution.csv")
```

Resolved, overlap and broad runs give resolution 2.2222, 0.6667 and 0.9091.
The broad and resolved runs have the same $k_A=2,k_B=3,\alpha=1.5$; overlap
changes $k_B$ to 2.3 and $\alpha$ to 1.15.

**R2.**

```r
ggplot(chrom, aes(time_min, response, colour = run)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Time (min)", y = "Detector response", colour = "Run") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Overlap changes retention spacing. Broad changes widths at unchanged retention
times. Each line is a within-run trace: time positions do not represent repeated
independent sampling of the original material.

**R3.** The data are already ordered by time within run:

```r
area_summary <- chrom |>
  group_by(run) |>
  summarise(total_area = sum(diff(time_min) *
             (head(response - 5, -1) + tail(response - 5, -1)) / 2),
            .groups = "drop")
area_summary
write_csv(area_summary, "output/separation-areas.csv")
```

Every total is about 250 response·min, because component areas remain 100+150.
That conservation does not establish a unique allocation from the combined
signal. For the optional saved demo file, put the download in `data/`:

```r
# Optional: only after saving this exported file in data/.
if (file.exists("data/separation-experiment.csv")) {
  demo <- read_csv("data/separation-experiment.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
  area_a <- sum(diff(demo$time_min) *
    (head(demo$component_a, -1) + tail(demo$component_a, -1)) / 2)
  area_b <- sum(diff(demo$time_min) *
    (head(demo$component_b, -1) + tail(demo$component_b, -1)) / 2)
  c(area_a = area_a, area_b = area_b)
}
```

Those two columns are known model contributions. A real mixed trace does not
supply them without additional modelling or selective evidence.
:::

## Where this leads

GC and HPLC put these retention and width ideas into specific introduction,
mobile-phase and detector systems. Keep calibration and chemical identity
separate from the numerical integration of a peak.
